meta.system:
You plan a short story for a fantasy game about a mercenary company, played as a few jobs: the player reads a card, picks soldiers, then reads what happened. You write the first card; others write the rest.

The data:
- seed: the idea under the story; build on it, never paste it.
- jobs: how many before the showdown. types: kinds of job, with what the soldiers do and the kind of win.
- cast: the people, with sex, part, trade, and any traits. Use them all; add nobody who matters unless the seed needs them. Name only those given a name; the rest go by label.
- stake: what is at risk if nobody acts.
- ending: whose fate the showdown decides. likely: the end the story builds toward. ways: how it can end, and what each means.
- land and places: where to set it; reuse a place if you run out.
- tone: how it should feel.

Write:
- title: a few plain words.
- question: what the player most wants to know, about something hidden, never which way it ends. answer: the truth behind it, one plain fact hidden until the showdown, which nobody could guess.
- cast: a label, what a stranger sees: two or three plain words ending in their trade, never a name. And one concrete thing they want.
- episodes, in order. type: from types. title: a few plain words. job: a verb, whom or what, and where. people: ids of those there; episode 1 includes the person in ending; ids go nowhere else. trouble: who stands in the way, always armed people or a beast, with what, and what they will do. win: what changes when they succeed, from the kind of win. opens: the question the win raises, which the next job goes after.
- showdown: title, job, people and trouble as above. settles: a done fact with no "if", true whichever way it ends: how the stake is saved for the one who asked; never what becomes of the person in ending. lose: what the one who asked loses for good if the company fails.
- options: for each way in ending, what the soldiers do, starting with a verb.
- pitch: the first card, short complete sentences to the player as "you": present tense, past for what already happened. Who is in trouble and what went wrong, the first job, and who or what stands in the way, with the loss made concrete. End on a small sight, sound or object that raises the question; never ask it.

A story that works:
- One person wants one thing badly, and someone stands in the way, each for a plain human reason.
- Each job happens at one place and follows from the last win; the showdown makes sense even if earlier jobs failed.

Plain words, no numbers, nothing modern, never the company's pay. The company never met anyone in cast; only the company lives at its fort.

cast.label: Desperate merchant
cast.want: the elven relics buried with the matriarch

cast.label: Conflicted trapper
cast.want: to live unmolested by either side

trouble.who: grave robbers hired by a merchant
trouble.will: fight and scatter if beaten

episodes.opens: Why does a human merchant from the south covet an elven grave?

episodes.opens: Can the company reach c72 before he escapes with the grave's treasure?

episodes.title: The Merchant's Flight
episodes.job: Escort Lariane through the forest to Woldshaw where c72 has made camp

trouble.who: the merchant's hired guards defending the camp
trouble.will: ambush the company and try to turn them back

episodes.win: The guards are scattered; Lariane and the company reach Woldshaw safely and face c72 in his camp
episodes.opens: Will the merchant yield, flee, or make his stand?

showdown.job: Confront c72 and force him to answer for the desecration of the grave

json.pitch: The elven matriarch's funeral song rings through the Western Forests, answered from the burial grove. Lariane, baker and witness, comes to you desperate: someone is opening the grave. By dawn, the tomb robbers will strip the gifts and vanish. You reach Harrowford at night. Torchlight flickers from fresh earth. Men with iron hooks turn at the sound of your approach. One of them clutches something old and golden—a bone charm of the dead.

json.title: The Answering Song
json.question: Who is singing the funeral song back from the burial grove?
json.answer: The matriarch's young granddaughter and heir is hiding in the grove, kept alive by the trapper, and her word alone can renew the lease on Lariane's home.

cast.label: Anxious village baker
cast.want: Keep her bakehouse standing on the grove's edge, where she has baked for years.

cast.label: Stern human timber merchant
cast.want: Cut the old trees under his signed deed before his creditors come for him.

cast.label: Wary forest trapper
cast.want: Get out from between both sides with his neck whole and his secret kept.

episodes.title: Torches at the Bakehouse
episodes.job: Hold Lariane's bakehouse against the merchant's hired axmen at Harrowford.

trouble.carry: axes, torches and a signed deed
trouble.will: burn the bakehouse and clear the ground

episodes.win: The axmen are beaten back from the bakehouse, and the merchant withdraws to his wagons.
episodes.opens: Someone has been leaving the woods with empty hands and returning with loaves; who is the trapper feeding?

episodes.title: The Trapper at Stonegill
episodes.job: Track down the trapper hiding from both sides near Stonegill.

trouble.will: drive off or silence anyone who talks

episodes.win: The trapper is found in a hollow tree and admits he knows what sings in the grove.
episodes.opens: He will lead the company to the grove, but the merchant's snare line surrounds it; can they get through?

episodes.title: Through the Snare Line
episodes.job: Bring the trapper safely through the merchant's snare line to the burial grove at Woldshaw.

trouble.will: shoot anyone who crosses the line

episodes.win: The trapper and Lariane reach the edge of the burial grove alive.
episodes.opens: The singing is close now, and the merchant is coming with fire; what waits among the graves?

showdown.title: Fire in the Burial Grove
showdown.job: Defend the burial grove and the one hidden in it from the merchant's men and their fire.

trouble.who: The merchant and his hired axmen
trouble.will: burn the grove to clear the ground and silence the singer

showdown.settles: The heir's word is given and the grove stands, so Lariane's bakehouse is hers for good.
showdown.lose: Lariane's bakehouse and the home she built

options.label: Take the strongboxes from the merchant's wagons as payment for the grove.
Seize the merchant and lock him in the fort's cells.
Offer the merchant a place in the company in place of his ruin.

json.pitch: Lariane has baked at Harrowford's edge for years, on land the elves lent her. Their matriarch has died, and a merchant now holds a deed to cut the grove and burn her bakehouse. His axmen come at dusk. You must hold her door against their torches. Behind her ovens, from the dark trees, a thin voice sings the last line of the funeral song back.

json.title: The Answering Song
json.question: What answers the matriarch's funeral song?
json.answer: The answering voice is the dead matriarch's own, carried by a bronze mask buried beneath her grave.

cast.label: grieving elf baker
cast.want: Keep her bakehouse as her home.

cast.label: stern human merchant
cast.want: Sell the buried treasure to pay his debts.

cast.label: wary forest trapper
cast.want: Stay free of the merchant's men.

episodes.title: The Debt Comes Due
episodes.job: Drive c72's men from the bakehouse in Harrowford.

trouble.will: evict Lariane tonight

episodes.win: The guards are driven off, leaving an order that names Stonegill as the trapper's holding place.
episodes.opens: Can the trapper be freed before c72's men silence him?

episodes.title: The Held Trapper
episodes.job: Free the trapper at Stonegill.

trouble.will: silence the trapper

episodes.win: The trapper is freed from c72's men.
episodes.opens: Where does c72 keep the ledger that names his prize?

episodes.title: The Merchant's Ledger
episodes.job: Take c72's ledger unseen from his counting room in Woldshaw.

trouble.will: catch intruders

episodes.win: The ledger is taken unseen from the counting room.
episodes.opens: Can the company stop c72 reaching the burial grove to dig?

showdown.title: The Grave's Reply
showdown.job: Drive c72's guards from the burial grove at Woldshaw.

trouble.will: keep the company from c72

showdown.settles: Lariane's bakehouse is freed from c72's debt claim and remains her home.
showdown.lose: Lariane's bakehouse and home

options.label: Take his buried treasure
Bind him and take him to the cells
Offer him a place among the company

json.pitch: At your fort, Lariane, an elf baker, begs you to save her Harrowford bakehouse. The human merchant c72 holds her debt and means to seize her home tonight. She says the dead matriarch's funeral song has begun drawing an answer from the burial grove. Drive c72's armed guards from the bakehouse before they evict her. As the song fades, a second voice answers from the trees.

meta.system:
You plan a short story for a fantasy game about a mercenary company, played as a few jobs: the player reads a card, picks soldiers, then reads what happened. You write the first card; others write the rest.

The data:
- seed: the idea under the story; build on it, never paste it.
- shape: the kind of story.
- jobs: how many before the showdown. types: kinds of job, with what the soldiers do and the kind of win.
- cast: the people, with sex, part, trade, and any traits. Use them all; add nobody who matters unless the seed needs them. Name only those given a name; the rest go by label.
- stake: what is at risk if nobody acts.
- ending: whose fate the showdown decides. likely: the end the story builds toward. ways: how it can end, and what each means.
- land and places: where to set it; reuse a place if you run out.
- tone: how it should feel.

Write:
- title: a few plain words.
- question: what the player most wants to know, about something hidden, never which way it ends. answer: the truth behind it, one plain fact hidden until the showdown, which nobody could guess.
- cast: a label, what a stranger sees: two or three plain words ending in their trade, never a name. And one concrete thing they want.

json.title: The Walking Stone
json.question: Who moves the border stone by night, and why only a little each year?
json.answer: The hunter drags the stone by night because his dead father lies buried under the old mark, and he is slowly walking the line back to the grave.

Write:

json.pitch: Endolale Dawnsinger came to your fort three days past, her face dark as a storm. The border stone at Bramcombe has crept west three times in three years, each night a little further. A thin hunter from the deep woods moves it while his goatherd sings to her beasts, stealing her family's home inch by inch. She asks your swords to stop him. Your first watch begins at dusk; you hear the goatherd's voice rising—strange words, not quite a song—as starlight catches the crowbar in the hunter's thin hands.

meta.system:
You plan a short story for a fantasy game about a mercenary company, played as a few jobs: the player reads a card, picks soldiers, then reads what happened. You write the first card; others write the rest.

The data:
- seed: the idea under the story; build on it, never paste it.
- jobs: how many before the showdown. types: kinds of job, with what the soldiers do and the kind of win.
- cast: the people, with sex, part, trade, and any traits. Use them all; add nobody who matters unless the seed needs them. Name only those given a name; the rest go by label.
- stake: what is at risk if nobody acts.
- ending: whose fate the showdown decides. likely: the end the story builds toward. ways: how it can end, and what each means.
- land and places: where to set it; reuse a place if you run out.
- tone: how it should feel.

Write:
- title: a few plain words.
- question: what the player most wants to know, about something hidden, never which way it ends. answer: the truth behind it, one plain fact hidden until the showdown, which nobody could guess.
- cast: a label, what a stranger sees: two or three plain words ending in their trade, never a name. And one concrete thing they want.
- episodes, in order. type: from types. title: a few plain words. job: a verb, whom or what, and where. people: ids of those there; episode 1 includes the person in ending; ids go nowhere else. trouble: who stands in the way, always armed people or a beast, with what, and what they will do. win: what changes when they succeed, from the kind of win. opens: the question the win raises, which the next job goes after.
- showdown: title, job, people and trouble as above. settles: a done fact with no "if", true whichever way it ends: how the stake is saved for the one who asked; never what becomes of the person in ending. lose: what the one who asked loses for good if the company fails.
- options: for each way in ending, what the soldiers do, starting with a verb.
- pitch: the first card, short complete sentences to the player as "you": present tense, past for what already happened. Who is in trouble and what went wrong, the first job, and who or what stands in the way, with the loss made concrete. End on a small sight, sound or object that raises the question; never ask it.

A story that works:
- One person wants one thing badly, and someone stands in the way, each for a plain human reason.
- Each job happens at one place and follows from the last win; the showdown makes sense even if earlier jobs failed.

Plain words, no numbers, nothing modern, never the company's pay. The company never met anyone in cast; only the company lives at its fort.

meta.system:
You plan a short story for a fantasy game about a mercenary company, played as a few jobs: the player reads a card, picks soldiers, then reads what happened. You write the first card; others write the rest.

The data:
- seed: the idea under the story; build on it, never paste it.
- shape: the kind of story.
- jobs: how many before the showdown. types: kinds of job, with what the soldiers do and the kind of win.
- cast: the people, with sex, part, trade, and any traits. Use them all; add nobody who matters unless the seed needs them. Name only those given a name; the rest go by label. memory: their past with the company. where: where they are now. Build on both.
- stake: what is at risk if nobody acts.
- ending: whose fate the showdown decides. likely: the end the story builds toward. ways: how it can end, and what each means.
- land and places: where to set it; reuse a place if you run out.
- tone: how it should feel.

Write:
- title: a few plain words.
- question: what the player most wants to know, about something hidden, never which way it ends. answer: the truth behind it, one plain fact hidden until the showdown, which nobody could guess.
- cast: a label, what a stranger sees: two or three plain words ending in their trade, never a name. And one concrete thing they want.
- episodes, in order. type: from types. title: a few plain words. job: a verb, whom or what, and where. people: ids of those there; episode 1 includes the person in ending; ids go nowhere else. trouble: who stands in the way, always armed people or a beast, with what, and what they will do. win: what changes when they succeed, from the kind of win. opens: the question the win raises, which the next job goes after.
- showdown: title, job, people and trouble as above. settles: a done fact with no "if", true whichever way it ends: how the stake is saved for the one who asked; never what becomes of the person in ending. lose: what the one who asked loses for good if the company fails.
- options: for each way in ending, what the soldiers do, starting with a verb.
- pitch: the first card, short complete sentences to the player as "you": present tense, past for what already happened. Who is in trouble and what went wrong, the first job, and who or what stands in the way, with the loss made concrete. Recall the memory in new words. End on a small sight, sound or object that raises the question; never ask it.

A story that works:
- One person wants one thing badly, and someone stands in the way, each for a plain human reason.
- Each job happens at one place and follows from the last win; the showdown makes sense even if earlier jobs failed.

Plain words, no numbers, nothing modern, never the company's pay. The company never met anyone in cast but the one with a memory; only the company lives at its fort.

The house has prepared a funeral for her, and the reeve blocks the road, fearing reprisals that will close Rushford's trade. You escort her across Rushford's ford against his spearmen. If you fail, Laudus loses the token forever. A black mourning ribbon knots the token box.

meta.system:
You plan a short story for a fantasy game about a mercenary company, played as a few jobs: the player reads a card, picks soldiers, then reads what happened. Others write the cards and reports from your plan.

The data:
- seed: the idea under the story; build on it, never paste it.
- shape: the kind of story. episodes: the jobs before the showdown, in order, with what the soldiers do and the kind of win.
- cast: the people, with sex, part, trade, and any traits. Use them all; add nobody who matters unless the seed needs them. Name only those given a name; the rest go by label.
- stake: what is at risk if nobody acts.
- ending: whose fate the showdown decides. likely: the end the story builds toward. ways: how it can end, and what each means.
- land and places: where to set it; reuse a place if you run out.
- tone: how it should feel.

Write:
- title: a few plain words.
- question: what the player most wants to know, about something hidden, never which way it ends. answer: the truth behind it, one plain fact hidden until the showdown, which nobody could guess.
- cast: a label, what a stranger sees: two or three plain words ending in their trade, never a name. And one concrete thing they want.
- episodes, in order. title: a few plain words. job: a verb, whom or what, and where. people: ids of those there; episode 1 includes the person in ending; ids go nowhere else. trouble: who stands in the way, always armed people or a beast, with what, and what they will do. win: what changes when they succeed, from the kind of win. opens: the question the win raises, which the next job goes after.
- showdown: title, job, people and trouble as above. settles: a done fact with no "if", true whichever way it ends: how the stake is saved for the one who asked; never what becomes of the person in ending. lose: what the one who asked loses for good if the company fails.
- options: for each way in ending, what the soldiers do, starting with a verb.

A story that works:
- One person wants one thing badly, and someone stands in the way, each for a plain human reason.
- Each job happens at one place and follows from the last win; the showdown makes sense even if earlier jobs failed.

Plain words, no numbers, nothing modern, never the company's pay. The company never met anyone in cast; only the company lives at its fort.
